props.name: basf 1923
props.note: history, cited from lit. 5 (Ind. Eng. Chem. 40, 2230, 1948)
props.statement: The high-pressure hydrogenation of CO (and/or CO2) was developed in Germany and applied commercially by B.A.S.F. as early as 1923 (lit. 5).

props.name: co hydrogenation chosen
props.statement: Only the hydrogenation of CO is considered for the plant.

props.name: cold gas and thermocouples
props.statement: The reactor temperature is controlled by adding cold synthesis gas between 6 separate catalyst beds; temperature control with thermocouples is fairly simple, so a rise can be compensated in time by adding more cold gas.

props.name: crude methanol impurities
props.statement: The crude methanol is mainly contaminated with water, dimethyl ether and higher alcohols; the plant yields 84 t/d methanol, 2 t/d dimethyl ether, 7 t/d 'voorloop' and 7 t/d bottoms (water + higher alcohols).

props.name: feed purified of COS and Fe(CO)4

evidence.note: '002~COS' read as 'CO2, COS' (uncertain); 'Fe ~' (CO)4'' = Fe(CO)4 as printed; quote withheld: sha256:40c41cd44346831d2e03e857585d894387b2c81cf5ca3b5b9fe25cb2701b7b3e chars:99

props.statement: The fresh feed, a CO-H2 mixture (2,2 - 2,4), is purified of impurities such as COS and 'Fe(CO)4' (the latter called a catalyst poison on p. 12) before it is compressed with the circulating gas.

props.name: hot co resistant materials
props.statement: The reactor and other apparatus in contact with hot CO must resist it, to prevent formation of the catalyst poison Fe(CO)4 and corrosion: heavily loaded parts of steel lined with a 2 mm bronze plate, lighter parts of a Cu-Mn alloy, hot lines of stainless steel (lit. 10); in the U.S.A. often only 18-8 stainless steel is used (lit. 2).

props.name: methanol difficult at 1 atm
props.statement: At 1 atm methanol formation is very difficult (ΔGr > 0); raising the pressure improves this, but the side reactions are still thermodynamically more probable, so methanol formation is only realizable with selective catalysts that establish this equilibrium faster than the others.

props.name: purge inerts
props.statement: Part of the gas leaving the separator is purged to keep the amount of inert gas constant; the rest returns to the reactor through the circulator.

props.name: synthesis gas raw materials
props.statement: The raw material for synthesis gas was at first coke (still 71 % in 1945); in 1948 77 % came from natural gas (in the U.S.A.). Coke, oil, or refinery and natural gas come into consideration as raw material for the synthesis gas CO + H2.

props.name: temperature effects

evidence.note: '40öf' is an illegible temperature; not recorded as a value; quote withheld: sha256:9d0841421f76d5447ff02a1fbb2880df6e6c0787477942cbbca4816f9666bd74 chars:143

props.statement: The ΔGr values show that the equilibrium is more favourable at lower temperature (but the rate is then too small) and that raising the temperature strongly promotes the formation of CH3OCH3; raising the temperature above a value printed '40öf' promotes especially the strongly exothermic CO + 3 H2 -> CH4 + H2O, which raises the temperature further; hence a good selective catalyst and very good control of the catalyst-bed temperature are needed.

props.name: us co co2 combination
props.statement: In the U.S.A. a combination of CO and CO2 is also used, because the reaction with CO2 is less exothermic so the chance of the temperature running away is smaller; a disadvantage is the water formed, which makes the purification more expensive.

props.name: usual conditions and catalysts
props.statement: The process rests on the equilibrium CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH and usually works at 250-350 atm and 350-380 °C; Zn, Cr, Mn or Al oxides are often used as catalysts; many side reactions are possible but the process is fairly well controllable provided temperature and pressure do not vary too much.
